extracted.intended_audience: seminarians, Catholic theology students, clergy, and scholars of Christian doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the Catholic doctrine of justification (sanctifying grace), its genesis as a multi-stage process, the nature and necessity of justifying faith, and the preparatory acts required alongside faith. Targets interpretation of Scripture, Tradition, and the Council of Trent against Protestant positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Faith for Justification
rubrics_metrics.description: “Faith is the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and the root of all justification.” (Council of Trent) — justifying faith is necessary for an adult to be disposed to justice and to receive sanctifying grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that faith initiates the process of justification and is required, but is not sufficient by itself in the sense claimed by some Reformers. Faith must be preceded by intellectual illumination and strengthening of the will (affectus credulitatis). The Council of Trent declares this position and anathematizes contrary assertions that reduce justifying faith to mere confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Justifying Faith: dogmatic (not fiduciary)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church teaches that the faith whereby man is justified is a dogmatic or theoretical belief in the truths of Divine Revelation, not merely a confident persuasion of one’s own righteousness (fiduciary faith).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the Reformers’ definition of faith as fiducia (trust in personal forgiveness). Uses Scripture and Tradition to argue that justifying faith is intellectual assent to revealed truths (e.g., belief that Jesus is the Christ). The Council of Trent anathematized the view that justifying faith is 'nothing else but confidence in the divine mercy.' Anti-pattern: treating πίστις in New Testament uniformly as fiduciary trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Faith (classifications and critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformers distinguished fides historica (belief that Christ came), fides miraculorum (trust for miracles), and fides promissionum (faith in divine promises), with subdivisions like fides generalis and fides specialis (fiducia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records these classifications to explain the Reformers’ position and then critiques them: many New Testament occurrences of πίστις do not mean fiduciary faith, and Tradition supports the Catholic understanding. Use these distinctions only with caution; the Catholic position emphasizes dogmatic belief over fiduciary categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fides explicita vs fides implicita; Necessitas medii vs necessitas praecepti
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes explicit (fides explicita) — an express, fully developed belief in revealed truths — from implicit faith (fides implicita). Distinguishes the necessity of a means (necessitas medii) from the necessity of a precept (necessitas praecepti).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: ordinarily it suffices to have explicit knowledge and firm assent to the more important dogmas and moral precepts (e.g., the Apostles’ Creed’s core articles, Commandments, necessary Sacraments, the Our Father); other revealed truths may be held implicitly. Necessitas medii binds even the ignorant without fault when an objective means is required for salvation, whereas necessitas praecepti rests on positive divine command and admits dispensation for invincible ignorance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal dogmas required by necessitas medii (existence of God and eternal retribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: All men, to be justified and saved, must explicitly believe at least two dogmas: the existence of God and eternal retribution (necessitas medii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes debate about whether the Trinity and the Incarnation are likewise necessitas medii; theologians differ. The most probable opinion presented is that explicit belief in the Trinity and Incarnation is not strictly necessary in all cases, though those entering the Church and converts with use of reason are ordinarily bound to such explicit belief (necessitas medii per accidens). The Holy Office decision (1703) requires missionaries to explain Trinity and Incarnation to adult converts when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Other Preparatory Acts Besides Faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification requires, in addition to faith, preparatory/dispositive acts such as fear of divine justice, hope in God’s mercy, charity (love), detestation of sin, and penitence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council of Trent condemns the proposition that faith alone (without these dispositions) justifies. Scriptural support is cited (e.g., Luke, Romans, James) showing works and dispositions dispose the soul for justification. Anti-pattern: interpreting 'justified by faith' to exclude these preparatory acts (the Protestant sola fide error).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fides formata vs fides informis (faith formed by charity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholastic distinction: fides formata (faith informed/formed by charity) truly justifies, whereas fides informis (bare/empty faith) does not. Faith must be 'faith that worketh by charity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Galatians V.6 and James II to support that faith without charity (love) is ineffective. Theological implication: converts’ faith must be animated by love and good works; mere intellectual assent without moral transformation is insufficient. Anti-pattern: regarding demons' belief as salvific—belief without love is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification as a Process (genesis of sanctifying grace)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justification of an adult is not instantaneous but proceeds through well-defined stages (the process of justification): preparation (illumination, contrition), faith, cooperation with grace, and growth in sanctifying grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: spiritual regeneration likened to fetal development and physical birth — preceded by travailing (fear, contrition). Faith does not arise ex nihilo; it grows after intellectual illumination and strengthening of the will (initia fidei). Pastoral implication: conversion often requires time and progressive dispositions; anti-pattern: expecting immediate, complete sanctification without preparatory movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of Scripture and Tradition; rejection of sola scriptura/sola fide
rubrics_metrics.description: The Catholic position relies on both Scripture and Tradition to define justifying faith and the process of justification; Protestant principles like sola scriptura and sola fide are criticized as inconsistent with biblical teaching and dangerous ethically/theologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative guidance: demonstrating contradictions within Protestantism (e.g., Luther’s interpolation of 'alone') and ethical objections (antinomian tendencies). Use Scripture (e.g., Mark, John, Romans, James, Hebrews) together with patristic citations (e.g., St. Augustine, St. Gregory, St. Fulgentius) and conciliar definitions (Trent) when evaluating doctrines of justification.
